summary.text: 吃 is analyzed as a mouth-related semantic element 口 plus a sound element. Its early documented meaning is halting speech; its familiar meaning “eat” belongs to a separate, later-attested history whose relation to 喫 and other graphs remains disputed. [ref027] [ref013] [ref017] [ref020]

formation.text: Phonosemantic: 口 contributes the speech-related meaning category, while the element identified in the older analysis as 气 supplies the sound. The received Shuowen entry gives this structure and defines the word as difficult or halting speech. The current right side resembles 乞, but its precise graphic path from 气 in 吃 has not been traced. [ref027] [ref017]

components.text: 口 is the left-side mouth element. In this compound it contributes the speech-related semantic category; its independent pictographic history does not make it a depicted scene within 吃. [ref027] [ref024]

The right side is written like 乞 in the modern graph; the older analysis names 气 as the sound element. 乞 and 气 share an earlier graph in their own history, but the dated graphic path within 吃 is unresolved. [ref027] [ref017] [ref028]

sound.text: In Zhengzhang-style Old Chinese, 吃 is reconstructed *kɯd and 乞 *kʰɯds or *kʰɯd: similar enough for a sound-series relation, though not identical. Modern Mandarin chī and qǐ differ. [ref032]

history.text: The received Shuowen analysis records 从口气聲 and a halting-speech definition. A Shiji passage describes Han Fei as 口吃, supporting the speech sense in the transmitted text. These records do not establish the earliest physical form of the whole graph. [ref027] [ref013] [ref015]

The familiar eating use is associated in the evidence with 吃 and 喫, but sources disagree about its earliest spelling and how the graphs relate. Proposed accounts include interchange, sound borrowing, and simplification; the evidence reviewed does not settle a sequence, so these should not be treated as an established graphic history. [ref017] [ref018] [ref019] [ref020]

uncertainties.text: No inspected primary paleographic evidence establishes the earliest physical attestation of 吃 or an oracle-bone or bronze form. Reports of Warring States ceramic and Western Han manuscript examples remain unverified leads. [ref015] [ref033]
The component analysis names 气, while the current right side resembles 乞. Evidence describes the separate history of 乞 and 气, but does not trace the exact dated shape changes in 吃. [ref017] [ref028]

The route from the speech word to the eating spelling remains disputed, as do the earliest eating examples and the relations among 吃, 喫, 齕 and related forms. Literary citation dates do not date surviving physical witnesses. [ref016] [ref019] [ref020]

senses.period: attested in the received Shiji text; physical witness dating unresolved
senses.text: The Shuowen entry defines 吃 as difficult or halting speech, and the transmitted Shiji passage describes Han Fei as 口吃. This supports the speech sense, not an eating sense. [ref027] [ref013]

Dictionaries document 吃 for swallowing food or drink and associate this use with 喫. The earliest spelling and the relationship between the eating and speech graphs are not settled by the reviewed evidence. [ref015] [ref017] [ref018] [ref020]

senses.period: later historical use; dating unresolved here
senses.text: The dossier lists “suffer, endure” among the character’s uses, and reports Yuan-text examples for 喫. It does not establish when or by what semantic path this use became associated with 吃. [ref006] [ref018]
吃 is commonly used for “eat”; the dossier also records “drink.” Its relation to the older documented speech sense remains unresolved. [ref006] [ref017]

limitations.text: The reviewed sources do not establish whether the eating use developed from the speech word, was borrowed between graphs for similar-sounding words, or arose through a separate graphic history. No semantic chain is asserted. [ref019] [ref020]

Additional senses such as absorbing, consuming, swallowing chess pieces, and undergoing are recorded, but the dossier does not provide enough chronology to connect them reliably to the earliest attested sense. [ref015]

overview.text: 吃 combines a mouth-related meaning element with a sound element. Its earliest supported meaning is halting speech; the familiar “eat” sense has a separate, disputed history. [ref027] [ref013] [ref020]

components.text: 口 supplies the speech-related meaning category. [ref027]
The right side resembles 乞; the older analysis names 气. Its exact graphic path in 吃 is unresolved. [ref027] [ref017]

takeaway.text: The eating sense is familiar today, but its relation to the older stammer sense and to 喫 is unresolved. [ref017] [ref020]

relationships.text: 口 contributes the speech-related semantic category in the traditional phonosemantic analysis. [ref027]
The older analysis names 气 as the sound element; the modern right side resembles 乞, and historical pronunciation comparison supports a sound-series relation. [ref027] [ref017] [ref032]
The Shuowen analysis explicitly names 气 as the sound element in 吃. [ref027]
